title: Complex class with overloaded + and *
statement:
Professor Naveen teaches signals and needs a small tool for complex numbers. The program has a class Complex with a real part and an imaginary part. The operator + adds two complex numbers, and the operator * multiplies two complex numbers. The function display prints a complex number in the form (real, imaginary).
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Formulas used: (a + bi) + (c + di) = (a + c) + (b + d)i; (a + bi) * (c + di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i
Input Format: One line: four integers a, b, c, d (real, imag of first; real, imag of second).
Output Format: Line 1: "Sum: " + (real, imag). Line 2: "Product: " + (real, imag).
Constraints: -100 <= a, b, c, d <= 100
easy: Overload + and * inside a Complex class so two complex numbers can be added and multiplied just like normal numbers, then print both results.
logic: Addition adds the real parts together and the imaginary parts together.
Multiplication uses (ac - bd) for the real part and (ad + bc) for the imaginary part.
display prints "(" << real << ", " << imag << ")" - note the comma and spaces.
operator+ and operator* each return a new Complex object.
algorithm: class Complex with int real, imag and a constructor Complex(int r, int i).
Complex operator+(Complex other): return Complex(real + other.real, imag + other.imag);
Complex operator*(Complex other): return Complex(real*other.real - imag*other.imag, real*other.imag + imag*other.real);
void display(): print in the (real, imag) form.
main: read a, b, c, d; build first(a,b) and second(c,d); print Sum and Product.
mistakes: Swapping the operands of the subtraction (bd - ac) or forgetting that i*i = -1 (so it MINUS ac... precisely: real = ac - bd).
Returning void from the operators - they must return Complex so the result can be stored.
Wrong display format: the output needs exactly "(4, 6)" with a comma and a space.

title: Device -> Phone -> SmartPhone multilevel inheritance
statement:
Anand works in a mobile factory. The program has three classes in three levels: the class Device has a brand, the class Phone is derived from Device and adds the storage in GB, and the class SmartPhone is derived from Phone and adds the operating system. The brand and the storage must be accessible inside the derived classes, but not outside the classes. Every constructor prints a message when an object is created, and every destructor prints a message when an object is destroyed. The function show of the class SmartPhone prints the brand, the storage, and the operating system.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: One line: string brand, int storage, string os.
Output Format: Lines 1-3: "Device Created: " + brand, "Phone Created: " + storage, "SmartPhone Created: " + os. Line 4: "Brand: ... , Storage: ... , OS: ...". Lines 5-7: destructor messages in reverse order (SmartPhone, Phone, Device).
Constraints: 1 <= length of brand, os <= 20 (no spaces); 1 <= storage <= 2048
easy: Three classes stacked in a chain. Creating a SmartPhone first builds the Device part, then the Phone part, then the SmartPhone part - and destruction happens exactly backwards.
logic: Device holds protected string brand; Phone adds protected int storage; SmartPhone adds string os.
Each constructor prints its own Created message AFTER calling its base constructor (base first!).
Destructors print in reverse: SmartPhone, Phone, Device.
show() reads brand and storage directly because they are protected.
algorithm: class Device: protected brand; Device(string b) prints "Device Created: "; ~Device() prints "Device Destroyed: ".
class Phone : public Device: Phone(string b, int s) : Device(b) { print "Phone Created: "; }
class SmartPhone : public Phone: SmartPhone(b, s, o) : Phone(b, s) { print "SmartPhone Created: "; }
show() prints Brand / Storage / OS on one line with ", " separators.
main: read input, create SmartPhone s(brand, storage, os), call s.show().
mistakes: Passing values to the base constructor in the member-initialiser list - Phone(b, s) : Device(b) is required, otherwise there is no Device() default constructor.
Printing the Created messages in the wrong order (derived first) - the base ALWAYS constructs first.
Making brand/storage private - derived classes could not use them; they must be protected.
note: Constructor/destructor ordering with inheritance is one of the most repeated exam patterns.

title: Overloaded function larger (int / double / three ints)
statement:
Kavitha is a shop owner who compares prices and quantities every day. The program has three functions with the same name larger. The first function takes two integers and returns the larger integer. The second function takes two doubles and returns the larger double. The third function takes three integers and returns the largest integer.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: three integers a, b, c. Line 2: two doubles x, y.
Output Format: Line 1: "Larger of two integers: " + max(a, b). Line 2: "Larger of two doubles: " + max(x, y) (2 decimals). Line 3: "Largest of three integers: " + max(a, b, c).
Constraints: -1000 <= a, b, c <= 1000; -1000.00 <= x, y <= 1000.00
easy: Three functions all named larger, distinguished by their parameter lists: (int, int), (double, double) and (int, int, int). The compiler picks the right one automatically.
logic: larger(int, int) returns the bigger of the two integers.
larger(double, double) works the same way for doubles.
larger(int, int, int) keeps a running maximum of three values.
fixed << setprecision(2) affects only the double line; integers still print without decimals.
algorithm: int larger(int a, int b): return a > b ? a : b (written with if).
double larger(double a, double b): same pattern.
int larger(int a, int b, int c): m = a; if (b > m) m = b; if (c > m) m = c; return m.
main: read a b c, then x y; set cout << fixed << setprecision(2); print the three lines calling larger with matching arguments.
mistakes: Calling larger(x, y) where x, y are ints - that calls the INT version; the double values must be read as doubles.
Expecting integers to print as 35.00: with fixed setprecision, an int still prints as 35 (the format flag does not change int printing).
Wrong output labels - copy them exactly, word for word.
note: The hidden test with -3.25 -7.5 checks negative doubles.

title: Cinema booking with exception throwing
statement:
Mukesh manages the online booking of a cinema hall. The program has a class Cinema that keeps the number of seats available. The function book reduces the number of available seats by the number of seats requested. If the number of seats requested is more than the number of seats available, the function must not change the number of seats and must throw the string "Not enough seats" as an exception. A booking of exactly the number of seats available is allowed. The main function handles the exception and prints the message of the error.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: One line: three integers total, r1, r2.
Output Format: For each booking: "Booked <r> seats" on success or "Error: Not enough seats". Last line: "Seats Left: " + remaining seats.
Constraints: 1 <= total <= 500; 1 <= r1, r2 <= 500
easy: Two booking attempts are processed in order. A booking bigger than the seats left throws an exception that main catches and prints; a failed booking does not change the seat count.
logic: book(int seats): if seats > available, throw string("Not enough seats"); otherwise subtract.
main loops over the two requests inside try/catch (catch string msg).
After each booking (or error), the loop continues - the second booking still happens after a failed first one.
Exactly equal booking is allowed: booking 10 of 10 leaves 0.
algorithm: class Cinema with private int available; constructor sets it.
void book(int seats): if (seats > available) throw string("Not enough seats"); available -= seats;
int getAvailable(): return available.
main: read total r1 r2; for k = 0..1: try { book; print "Booked <r> seats"; } catch (string msg) { print "Error: " + msg; }
Print "Seats Left: " + getAvailable().
mistakes: Putting both bookings in ONE try block - the first failure would skip the second booking; each booking needs its own try/catch.
Using > for a valid booking or <= for throwing - booking exactly all seats must SUCCEED.
Forgetting to reset nothing: a failed booking leaves the seat count unchanged (that is the point of throwing before subtracting).
note: Sample 30 25 10 -> Booked 25, Error, Seats Left: 5 verifies the 'continue after error' logic.

title: Employee / Manager / Intern virtual salary through base pointers
statement:
Geetha prepares the salary statement of a company. The program has a base class Employee with a name and a base pay. Two classes are derived from it: Manager, which has a bonus and whose salary is the base pay plus the bonus, and Intern, whose salary is half of the base pay. Every class has its own version of the function salary. The statement is printed through pointers of the base class Employee, and for every employee the salary function of the actual object must be used.
The given code has errors, and it does not produce the correct output. Debug the code so that it works as described.
Input Format: Line 1: string n1, double b1, double bonus (manager). Line 2: string n2, double b2 (intern).
Output Format: Line 1: manager name + ": " + salary (2 decimals). Line 2: intern name + ": " + salary (2 decimals).
Constraints: 1 <= length of names <= 20 (no spaces); 1000.00 <= b1, bonus, b2 <= 100000.00
easy: A base-class pointer array holds a Manager and an Intern; calling salary() through the pointers must run the DERIVED versions - that needs virtual.
logic: Employee::salary() is declared virtual so dynamic binding happens.
Manager::salary() returns base + bonus; Intern::salary() returns base / 2.
main stores Employee* pointers to both objects and calls list[k]->salary().
Without virtual, both calls would print the raw base pay - the classic bug being debugged.
algorithm: class Employee: protected name, base; constructor; getName(); virtual double salary() { return base; }
class Manager : public Employee: Manager(...) : Employee(n, b) { bonus = bo; } ; salary() returns base + bonus.
class Intern : public Employee: salary() returns base / 2.
main: create Manager m and Intern i; Employee* list[2] = {&m, &i}; loop printing getName() + ": " + salary() with fixed setprecision(2).
mistakes: Forgetting the virtual keyword - then both lines print the base pay (wrong).
Dividing an int by 2 for the intern - base is double so base / 2 keeps decimals.
Calling salary() on the objects directly instead of through the base pointers (the task requires the pointer mechanism).
note: Hidden tests like Hari 38000.25 1999.75 -> 40000.00 verify rounding.

title: Professor: multiple inheritance from Teacher and Researcher
statement:
Dr. Ramesh works in the accounts section of a university. A professor is both a teacher and a researcher. A teacher has a salary, and a researcher has a number of published research papers. The university pays a bonus for every published paper, and the total pay of a professor is the salary plus the bonus for all the papers. Write a program that defines a class Teacher with a protected salary, a class Researcher with a protected number of papers, and a class Professor that is derived from both of them. Read the details of a professor, and print the salary, the number of papers, and the total pay.
Formula used: Total Pay = Salary + (Number of papers * Bonus per paper)
Input Format: One line: double salary, int papers, double bonus.
Output Format: Line 1: "Salary: " (2 decimals). Line 2: "Papers: " (integer). Line 3: "Total Pay: " (2 decimals).
Constraints: 10000.00 <= salary <= 500000.00; 0 <= papers <= 100; 0.00 <= bonus <= 10000.00
easy: A Professor inherits from two base classes at once (multiple inheritance) and computes total pay = salary + papers * bonus.
logic: Teacher holds the salary; Researcher holds the papers; both members are protected.
class Professor : public Teacher, public Researcher gets access to both.
totalPay(bonusPerPaper) = salary + papers * bonusPerPaper.
Print salary and papers first, then the total.
algorithm: class Teacher { protected: double salary; public: void setSalary(double s); };
class Researcher { protected: int papers; public: void setPapers(int p); };
class Professor : public Teacher, public Researcher with totalPay() and show(bonusPerPaper).
main: read salary, papers, bonus; cout << fixed << setprecision(2); create Professor p; setSalary; setPapers; p.show(bonus).
mistakes: Forgetting the comma-separated base list: public Teacher, public Researcher.
Printing papers with decimals - it is an int.
Integer overflow or wrong formula order: bonus is per paper, so multiply BEFORE adding.
note: 0 papers must still work: total = salary only (hidden test 30000.0 0 1000.0).

title: Division report with try/catch for divide by zero
statement:
Vasanth is a data entry operator who prepares a division report from pairs of numbers. For every pair, he divides the first number by the second number and records the whole-number quotient. A division by zero is not possible, so a pair with a zero divisor must not stop the report. For such a pair, an error must be recorded, and the report must continue with the next pair. Write a program that reads the pairs of numbers, throws an exception when the divisor is zero, handles the exception, and prints the report line for every pair.
Input Format: Line 1: integer n. Line 2: 2n integers (a b for each pair).
Output Format: n lines: "a / b = q" for success, or "a / b : Error: Division by zero" for a zero divisor.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 20; 0 <= a, b <= 10000
easy: Divide each pair and print the quotient; when the divisor is 0, throw an exception, catch it, print an error line, and keep going with the next pair.
logic: A helper divide(a, b) throws 0 (an int) when b == 0, else returns a / b.
Each pair is processed in its OWN try block so the loop never stops.
catch (int code) prints the error line with the exact wording.
algorithm: int divide(int a, int b): if (b == 0) throw 0; return a / b;
Read n; loop i = 1..n: read a, b.
try { q = divide(a, b); print a << " / " << b << " = " << q; }
catch (int code) { print a << " / " << b << " : Error: Division by zero"; }
mistakes: Wrapping the WHOLE loop in one try/catch - a failure would skip the remaining pairs; every pair needs its own try.
Printing the error inside divide() - the function should THROW, and main should print.
Using if (b == 0) with cout "Error" and no throw - the task explicitly requires throw/catch.
note: 0 / 3 = 0 is valid (zero numerator is fine); 0 / 0 is an error (zero divisor).

title: Score class with overloaded prefix ++ and --
statement:
Sundar operates the scoreboard of a school quiz. The score starts from a given value, and then he enters a series of commands. A command '+' adds 1 point to the score, and a command '-' removes 1 point from the score, but the score can never become less than 0, so a '-' command is ignored when the score is 0. The scoreboard also remembers the highest score that was reached, which includes the starting score. Write a program that defines a class Score and overloads the prefix operators ++ and -- for it. Both the operators return the same object using the this pointer. Apply all the commands in the given order, and print the final score and the highest score.
Input Format: Line 1: integer start. Line 2: string commands (only '+' and '-').
Output Format: Line 1: "Final Score: " + final. Line 2: "Highest Score: " + highest reached (starting score counts).
Constraints: 0 <= start <= 1000; 1 <= length of commands <= 100
easy: Process + and - commands on a Score object whose ++ and -- operators are overloaded; the object also remembers the highest value ever reached.
logic: operator++ adds 1, updates highest if needed, and returns *this (Score&).
operator-- subtracts 1 ONLY when value > 0, and returns *this.
highest starts at the starting score (the start itself counts).
main applies ++ for '+' and -- for '-' in command order.
algorithm: class Score with int value, highest; constructor Score(int start) sets both.
Score& operator++(): value++; if (value > highest) highest = value; return *this;
Score& operator--(): if (value > 0) value--; return *this;
main: read start and commands; loop: if '+' then ++s else --s;
Print "Final Score: " << s.getValue() and "Highest Score: " << s.getHighest().
mistakes: Ignoring the floor rule: '-' at score 0 must do NOTHING (highest stays, value stays).
Forgetting the starting score counts as the initial highest (see 0 / --+ -> Highest 1... actually highest becomes 1 only after the +; but start 2 / --- -> Highest 2).
Using postfix operators (s++) instead of prefix (++s) or returning void - the task demands prefix and *this.

title: Abstract Payment class with virtual destructor
statement:
Jayanthi works for an online shop that accepts payments in two ways: by card and by UPI. The gateway charges a fee for every payment. The fee for a card payment is 2.0 percent of the amount, and the fee for a UPI payment is 0.5 percent of the amount. Write a program that defines an abstract class Payment that cannot be used to create objects directly, with a function to calculate the fee, a function to print the name of the method, and a destructor. Define two concrete classes CardPayment and UpiPayment that are derived from it. Create the payment object for the method chosen, using a pointer of the base class, and delete the object through the same pointer. When the object is deleted, the destructor of the derived class must run first, and then the destructor of the base class. The destructor of the class CardPayment prints "Card Closed", the destructor of the class UpiPayment prints "UPI Closed", and the destructor of the class Payment prints "Payment Closed".
Formulas used: Fee = Amount * Rate / 100; Total = Amount + Fee
Input Format: One line: int choice (1 = card, 2 = UPI), double amount.
Output Format: Line 1: "Method: Card" or "Method: UPI". Line 2: "Fee: " (2 decimals). Line 3: "Total: " (2 decimals). Lines 4-5: destructor messages, derived first, then base.
Constraints: 1 <= choice <= 2; 100.00 <= amount <= 100000.00
easy: An abstract Payment class with pure virtual functions; the chosen payment type is created with new, used through a Payment* pointer, then deleted - the destructors print in derived-then-base order because the base destructor is virtual.
logic: Payment has virtual double fee(double) = 0; virtual void name() = 0; and virtual ~Payment() printing "Payment Closed".
CardPayment fee = amount * 2.0 / 100; UpiPayment fee = amount * 0.5 / 100.
new creates the right object; delete p runs the derived destructor first (virtual!), then the base one.
Total = amount + fee.
algorithm: Read choice and amount.
Payment* p = (choice == 1) ? new CardPayment() : new UpiPayment();
cout << fixed << setprecision(2); p->name(); print Fee and Total.
delete p; -> prints "Card Closed" or "UPI Closed", then "Payment Closed".
Return 0.
mistakes: Forgetting virtual on ~Payment() - then only "Payment Closed" prints (derived destructor skipped).
Trying Payment p; - an abstract class cannot be instantiated (that is the compile error in the buggy code).
Computing fee twice with different rounding - call p->fee(amount) and reuse it for both lines to keep them consistent.
note: Source note: the first display of sample 2 in the QB cuts off after 'UPI Closed'; the repeated block and hidden tests confirm the full output 'UPI Closed' + 'Payment Closed'.
